newsitem.title: UK: Europe grain traders hope slow market has seen low.
newsitem.headline: Europe grain traders hope slow market has seen low.

text.p: European grain traders ended the week hoping they had seen the bottom of the market after a series of falls.
But volume remains limited, while the market awaits the harvest, and the EU moves to get the new crop year's exporting underway.
And rain meant that traders began to worry about crop quality, especially on barley.
New-crop French prices mostly slipped but trade was slack during another week when the European Union stayed off the world export market and dealers assessed the new summer harvest.

Despite Saudi Arabia's one million tonne barley purchase, which was no surprise to the market on Thursday, feed barley prices eased on mounting crop quality fears after steady rain fell in the past week.

Traders said wet weather in northwest Europe, which could leave some malting barley below the quality threshold for malting, coupled with possible surpluses in eastern Europe, could foul up the bullish picture for barley this year.

However the prices to Saudi Arabia of as low as $120, on a fob equivalent basis, would need a subsidy for September shipment of some 26 Ecus per tonne for licences issued in August. And there were no signs yet the Commission was willing to drop its bullish view on barley when it came into the market.
Barley at Dunkirk, where Saudi shipments are often loaded, was quoted at 840 francs per tonne excluding carrying charges for September onwards.

The carrying charges applying uniquely to the French domestic trading system changed this week. For example the charges, derived from EU monthly storage increments, were 10.91 francs for first-half September in 1996/97 (July/June).
But an EU decision on Wednesday to cut the base increment by nine percent to one Ecu a tonne implies a cut in the French charge for the same period of 1997/98 to 9.92 francs a tonne.

In Britain there were signs that prices have finally got low enough to bring out some interest. Old crop futures bottomed out at 77 stg at the start of the week and physical traders reported a shortage of sellers at current levels, but plenty of would-be buyers.
A strong sterling made British feed wheat exports uncompetitive, traders said, particularly against Danish competition.
German grain prices have taken another knock this week but brokers think they could have bottomed out in both the delivered and export markets.
"Sellers will resist any further attempts to push prices lower. They would rather store the grain indefinitely," one broker said.
Sellers fob prices of old and new crop grain were steady or 2.50-5.00 marks a tonne down on the week, with business very limited due to consumer absence.
Traders said sellers were desperate for Brussels to reopen export subsidy tenders, especially for barley shipments to Saudi Arabia, but an EU move might still be weeks away.
Germany's 1997 grain crop may be at last year's 42 million tonnes or slightly higher and this should keep a lid on prices.
But although the weather is not unfavourable, there are some question marks on yields after an extremely cold spring and damage from lodging is not ruled out if it rains during harvesting.
Old crop wheat costs 270-320 marks in the fob market and new crop wheat is in a 267.50-305 marks range.
Prices are down by 20 marks from last year.
Benchmark 13 percent protein wheat is just under 280.
Spanish wheat prices varied widely as quality ranged from the very good to the very bad and overall trading was thin amid short supply, dealers said.

Continual rain in the northern region is delaying the harvest collection and prompting fears that wheat and barley crop quality and specific weights will be worsened, although it may yet be too early to determine the specific effect.

"It's not so much that there's been heavy rain, its just that it's been continual and so people start to worry about quality. Barley is more resistant than wheat, but still the weather has not really been good news," said a trader in the north of Spain.

Italian soft wheat was not traded on the Turin exchange because the market is waiting for the new product, but in the less important Mantova market, first indication for soft wheat prices ranged from 265,000 to 292,000 lire per tonne.
Also this week, durum wheat was not traded in Milan as the market waited for the new product.
